theme: Hananiah; the letter to the exiles, seek the city’s peace
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 28:1-29:32. A false prophet breaks Jeremiah’s yoke, and Jeremiah writes a letter to the exiles. Pay close attention to 29:4-14. This is one of the most important passages in the Bible on how to live in a foreign place.
settingTheScene: In 594 BC, a few years after the first exile, a prophet named Hananiah announced in the temple that Babylon’s power would be broken in two years. Jeremiah answered, and then Hananiah died. Meanwhile, the exiles in Babylon were being told by false prophets that their stay would be short. Jeremiah sent them a letter with a different message: settle in, because you will be there for seventy years.
observation: “Thus says the LORD of hosts… I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon” (28:2).
“The prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet” (28:9).
“You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron” (28:13).
“Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters” (29:5-6).
“But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare” (29:7).
“For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope” (29:11).
“You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (29:13).
interpretation:
Hananiah’s prophecy was exactly what the people wanted to hear. Jeremiah’s first response is irony: “Amen! May the LORD do so.” He would love for the prophecy to be true. But he reminds Hananiah that true prophets have always spoken of war, famine, and plague, and a message of peace must be proved by its fulfillment. Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke from Jeremiah’s neck, and God replaces it with one of iron. Hananiah dies within two months. A message that contradicts God’s word is not only wrong but dangerous.

Chapter 29 is the exiles’ letter. It must have been a surprise. They were hoping to go home soon. Instead, Jeremiah says to settle: build houses, plant gardens, marry, and have children. Do not shrink. Even more surprising: “Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf.” Pray for Babylon! Because in its welfare is your welfare. The people of God are called to be faithful and good neighbors in a place that is not their home.

Then comes the famous promise, 29:11, so often quoted alone. Read in context, it is not a promise of quick comfort. It was given to people who would spend seventy years in exile. The plans are for welfare and a future, but the timeline is long. The next verses give the way: call on me, pray, seek me with all your heart, and I will be found.

This is an important teaching for all Christians, since we are exiles and sojourners. We are not to withdraw, and we are not to be absorbed. We are to build, plant, pray, and wait for the promised return.
connection: 1 Peter 2:11-17 calls believers “sojourners and exiles” who are to honor everyone and live good lives among the Gentiles. 1 Timothy 2:1-2 urges prayer for kings and all in authority. Matthew 7:15-23 warns against false prophets. Hebrews 11:13-16 says that the faithful were strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a better country. John 17:15-18 shows Jesus praying that his disciples be kept in the world, not removed from it.
application:
Pray for your city and its leaders by name this week, including those you disagree with.

Think about how you can build and plant where you are rather than waiting for something better.

Read Jeremiah 29:11 with 29:10 and 29:13, and trust that God’s plans are long and good.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his plans for welfare and a future and hope.
Ask him to teach you to seek the welfare of where you live.
Ask him for patience in the waiting.
